newsitem.title: USA: New study shows a drop in television violence.
newsitem.headline: New study shows a drop in television violence.

text.p: Major U.S. television networks aired less violence in the latest season after several offending series were either cancelled or cleaned up, according to a study released on Tuesday.

But the study, by the UCLA Centre for Communication Policy, also cited continued high levels of violence in made-for-TV movies and theatrical films on TV. It singled out the independent channel UPN for airing almost as many offending series as all the other networks combined.

The UPN channel, jointly owned by Viacom Inc and Chris-Craft Industries Inc, broadcast four series deemed to raise frequent concerns about violence, it said. That compared with five offending series from the 181 hours of weekly programming produced by the four major television networks.
UPN, by comparison, runs only six hours of original programming per week.
The University of California at Los Angeles study also attacked UPN for actively promoting its violence, with the tag "Lethal Wednesday" for its bloodiest night of programming.

The study, funded by ABC, NBC, CBS and Fox, monitored every network prime time and Saturday morning entertainment programme aired in the 1995-96 television season. It also surveyed local and syndicated television, public television, basic and pay cable, home video, video games played on television and the new UPN and WB independent channels.
"Violence on television is still a serious problem," said Jeff Cole, director of the UCLA Centre for Communication Policy. "But in no way has network television gotten worse."

Cole said he believed the government played a role in the improvement and cited two summits on the matter hosted by President Bill Clinton as well as speeches by Republican presidential contender Bob Dole.

Since the issue of violence in television entered the political debate, legislation has passed requiring new television sets be equipped with "V-chips" enabling parents to scramble offensive programmes. Clinton also signed legislation this summer requiring networks to air at least three hours per week of educational programming.

Cole said the UCLA study aimed to examine violence in context and took particular issue with violence that ran at an early hour, did not include warnings, was not integral to the story line, was more graphic than it needed to be or did not feature the consequences.
"We don't simply lump 'Friday the Thirteenth' together with "'Schindler's List,'" he said. "Some violence is instrumental in sending an anti-violent message."

For that reason, he said, the study favoured ABC's "NYPD Blue," which it found to be responsible in its use of violence, over programmes like ABC's "America's Funniest Home Videos," which presented real-life clips of serious injuries as a laughing matter.

Overall, the study found the total number of series that posed frequent concerns about violence dropped to five in the latest season from nine the year before. In addition, there were four children's television series of concern, down from seven the year before. Children's shows cited for the most concern were "Teen-age Mutant Ninja Turtles" (CBS), "X-Men" (Fox) and "Power Rangers Zeo," Fox's reinvented "Mighty Morphin Power Rangers" series, and "Masked Rider" (Fox).
These programmes, the study said, "are little more than vehicles designed to showcase martial arts combat and are thus 'violence for the sake of violence.'"
While a drop was also tracked in violence in theatrical films shown on television, the study found they still offered "the most intense and disturbing violence on television."

Among the series it cited for removing disturbing violence since last year were "Lois & Clark" (ABC), "The X-Files" (Fox), "America's Most Wanted" (Fox), "Rescue 911" (CBS) and "Unsolved Mysteries" (NBC).
